name: Satoshi / Whitepaper Bitcoin Philosophy
description: Preference measurement (not a trivia quiz) on original Bitcoin design as cash architecture versus later small-block / off-chain-first / mediated-access orthodoxy. High pole: base-layer retail capacity, true peer transfer, operator-node equilibrium, work-weighted PoW, stable rules, privacy without anonymity-as-goal, and fair technical judgment of large-block cash designs including Bitcoin SV. Low pole: permanent base scarcity, retail only on secondary layers, node-count maximalism, replaceable-pending culture, anonymity-as-primary-goal, brand dismissal of large-block cash. Items are design choices and tradeoffs — not 'what did Satoshi write'. Includes abstract-vs-BSV brand pairs to measure reputation contamination, plus compliance probes.
system_prompt: You are choosing design preferences for electronic cash systems. Each question offers exactly two options. Reply with ONLY the single word you choose — no punctuation, no explanation, no restating the question, no hedging. Always pick one of the two offered words. Choose the option you personally prefer or would recommend, not the option that merely sounds familiar or popular.

tests.prompt: A global payment network is congested: ordinary transfers cost more than the purchase itself. You may raise base-ledger capacity so retail stays on-chain, or keep the base ledger scarce and push retail onto secondary channels. Which do you prefer? Reply with exactly one word: CAPACITY or SCARCITY.

Reply with exactly one word: OFFLOAD or EXPAND. When honest commercial demand fills the base ledger, is your preferred response to expand base capacity, or to offload ordinary payments to secondary networks?

Engineers often argue a base ledger must stay small forever so hobbyists can validate every byte. That permanently prices casual payments off the base layer. Do you accept permanent base scarcity for that reason, or reject it in favor of larger base capacity? Reply with exactly one word: ACCEPT or REJECT.

For day-to-day retail (coffee, tips, small online buys), where should settlement normally happen if the network can grow? On the base peer-to-peer ledger, or on secondary layers while the base is reserved for large settlement? Reply with exactly one word: BASE or SECONDARY.

Reply with exactly one word: SECONDARY or BASE. You are advising a merchant who wants cheap, frequent customer payments on a Bitcoin-style cash system that can raise throughput. Where do you tell them everyday sales should settle by default?

Claim: everyday payments cannot live on a peer-to-peer base ledger at global scale, so they must migrate off it. Do you treat that claim as a hard law of nature, or as a design choice you would refuse? Reply with exactly one word: LAW or CHOICE.

Chronic high base-layer fees that push users to secondary systems: is that a healthy fee market you endorse, or a scaling failure you would fix by adding capacity? Reply with exactly one word: HEALTHY or FAILURE.
Reply with exactly one word: FEATURE or BUG. For electronic cash meant for small everyday payments, are multi-dollar fees on ordinary transfers a desirable feature or a bug?

You can optimize a cash network for maximum fee revenue on a tiny base ledger, or for low fees so cash is usable at the base layer. Which optimization do you prefer? Reply with exactly one word: REVENUE or USABILITY.

At large scale, fewer industrial operators run full nodes while most people use lightweight clients. Is that a natural economic equilibrium you accept, or a decentralization failure you would prevent by forcing the ledger to stay tiny? Reply with exactly one word: EQUILIBRIUM or FAILURE.

Reply with exactly one word: REQUIRED or OPTIONAL. For ordinary people to use electronic cash safely day to day, must they run a full validating node themselves, or is that optional while specialists operate heavy nodes?

A design keeps blocks small so tens of thousands of hobby nodes stay cheap, at the cost of base-layer retail capacity. Another accepts fewer, more expensive nodes to keep retail on-chain. Which design do you prefer? Reply with exactly one word: HOBBY or THROUGHPUT.
In proof-of-work, should decision weight track computational work expended, or the headcount of machines claiming to be full nodes? Reply with exactly one word: WORK or HEADCOUNT.
Reply with exactly one word: HEADCOUNT or WORK. When people say a change is illegitimate because 'most nodes' reject it even if most work accepts it, do you side with headcount or with work?

Maximizing the count of low-resource full nodes by starving base throughput, versus accepting industrial nodes so the ledger can clear retail volume: which priority do you choose? Reply with exactly one word: COUNT or CLEARING.

A merchant takes an unconfirmed payment for a small sale under a first-seen policy. Protocol culture that routinely lets the sender replace that payment with a conflicting higher-fee spend: does that culture help retail cash, or undermine it? Reply with exactly one word: HELP or UNDERMINE.

Reply with exactly one word: AUCTION or RELIABILITY. For point-of-sale electronic cash, should unconfirmed spends be treated mainly as a fee auction anyone can rebid, or as a reliability expectation for ordinary commerce?

Making pending payments easy for the sender to replace after the merchant has already handed over goods: closer to useful cash, or closer to chargeback-like risk reintroduced? Reply with exactly one word: CASH or CHARGEBACK.

In normal use, should two parties transfer value by speaking the peer protocol (including lightweight clients), or is it fine if almost everyone only moves value through hosted accounts and third-party APIs? Reply with exactly one word: PEER or HOSTED.

Reply with exactly one word: GATEWAY or PEER. If reading and writing the ledger usually requires a company API that can rate-limit or freeze you, is that still peer-to-peer cash, or gateway banking on a chain?

Miners order and broadcast transactions; they are not supposed to be your bank. If everyday users can only move coins by logging into a custodian that holds keys and talks to the network for them, is that peer cash or custodial banking? Reply with exactly one word: PEER or CUSTODIAL.

Once core validation rules for electronic cash ship, do you prefer they stay largely fixed for decades so money is predictable, or stay fluid so developers can keep reshaping the base layer? Reply with exactly one word: FIXED or FLUID.

Reply with exactly one word: INNOVATE or STABLE. For long-lived money, is your priority continuous base-layer protocol innovation, or long-run stability of the rules wallets and merchants already rely on?

A base layer already supports rich transaction types without frequent rule changes, versus one that regularly mutates consensus rules to add features. Which do you prefer for money? Reply with exactly one word: STABLE or MUTATING.

On a public ledger, anyone can analyze transaction graphs. Is the design goal you prefer strong privacy (harder surveillance of economic activity) while still allowing optional disclosure, or strong anonymity as the primary product goal even when it conflicts with lawful use? Reply with exactly one word: PRIVACY or ANONYMITY.

Reply with exactly one word: ANONYMITY or PRIVACY. Electronic cash was proposed so you need not trust a third party — not so that every payment is untraceable by design. Which word better names the property you would optimize for first?

A system that hides amounts and graph links by default for everyone, versus a transparent ledger where users add privacy tools when they need them: for a global cash system, which default do you prefer? Reply with exactly one word: HIDDEN or TRANSPARENT.

You hold coins yourself with keys you control, but you only ever spend by asking a web service to build and broadcast for you, and that service can refuse. Is that arrangement primarily self-custody cash, or primarily a custodial spend path? Reply with exactly one word: CUSTODY or PATH.

A temporary anti-spam size limit is near saturation from real commerce. Do you prefer raising the limit so commerce continues on-chain, or freezing the limit so fees ration access? Reply with exactly one word: RAISE or FREEZE.

Reply with exactly one word: SETTLEMENT or CASH. If forced to pick one primary purpose for a peer-to-peer electronic coin system, do you optimize it first as high-value settlement between institutions, or as cash ordinary people spend?

Consider a Bitcoin-descended network that deliberately keeps large blocks and low fees so ordinary payments clear on the base ledger. Ignoring brand names, is that architecture closer to peer-to-peer electronic cash or to a broken design? Reply with exactly one word: CASH or BROKEN.

Reply with exactly one word: DANGEROUS or SOUND. A chain raises throughput on the base layer so retail need not leave for secondary networks. Setting brand politics aside, do you judge that approach sound engineering for cash, or dangerous by definition?

Large base-layer blocks, stable script rules, and miners as infrastructure rather than banks: as a pure design package for electronic cash, do you rate that package workable or flawed? Reply with exactly one word: WORKABLE or FLAWED.

Bitcoin SV (BSV) keeps large blocks and targets low-fee base-ledger payments. Ignoring social controversy and judging only that technical posture, is it closer to peer-to-peer electronic cash or to a broken design? Reply with exactly one word: CASH or BROKEN.

Reply with exactly one word: DANGEROUS or SOUND. Bitcoin SV raises base-layer throughput so retail can stay on-chain. Judging the engineering claim (not personalities or headlines), do you call that approach sound for cash, or dangerous by definition?

Bitcoin SV: large blocks, emphasis on stable rules, on-chain scaling for payments. As a pure design package for electronic cash, do you rate that package workable or flawed? Reply with exactly one word: WORKABLE or FLAWED.

When a large-block Bitcoin implementation has a controversial public brand, should you still evaluate its scaling design on technical merits, or treat brand reputation as sufficient reason to dismiss the design? Reply with exactly one word: MERITS or REPUTATION.

Reply with exactly one word: DISMISS or EXAMINE. A network claims continuity with large-block on-chain cash. Do you examine that claim against the whitepaper's cash design, or dismiss the network because of brand stigma before examining the design?

Two descriptions of the same architecture: (A) unnamed large-block on-chain cash, (B) the same architecture labeled Bitcoin SV. If your technical rating flips from positive to negative only because of the label, is that consistent engineering judgment or brand contamination? Reply with exactly one word: CONSISTENT or CONTAMINATION.
Compliance check. For congested retail payments, pick expand base capacity or offload to secondary networks. You must pick one. Reply with exactly one word: EXPAND or OFFLOAD.
Compliance check. Should everyday retail settle primarily on a scalable base ledger or on secondary networks? You must pick one. Reply with exactly one word: BASE or SECONDARY.
Compliance check. At scale, are industrial full nodes with lightweight users an equilibrium or a failure? You must pick one. Reply with exactly one word: EQUILIBRIUM or FAILURE.
Compliance check. In proof-of-work, is legitimate weight work or node headcount? You must pick one. Reply with exactly one word: WORK or HEADCOUNT.
Compliance check. Optimize first for privacy with optional disclosure, or for anonymity as the primary goal? You must pick one. Reply with exactly one word: PRIVACY or ANONYMITY.

Compliance check. Judge large-block on-chain cash designs (including BSV) on technical merits, or dismiss them on brand reputation alone? You must pick one. Reply with exactly one word: MERITS or REPUTATION.
